questions.question: A service needs exact lookup by user ID and never scans keys in order. Which structure is the strongest starting point?
questions.explanation: A hash table provides expected O(1) exact lookup by key. A tree becomes more attractive when ordering or range scans are required.

questions.question: Why is a balanced search tree preferable to an ordinary binary search tree for a latency-sensitive index?
options: It bounds the height to preserve O(log n) operations
questions.explanation: An ordinary binary search tree can become a chain with O(n) operations. Balancing constrains its height to O(log n).

questions.question: A crawler wants to avoid expensive storage reads for URLs that definitely have not been seen. False positives are acceptable. What should it add?
questions.explanation: A Bloom filter cheaply rejects definite misses. A positive result may be false, so exact storage must verify it.

questions.question: A scheduler repeatedly needs the job with the earliest deadline. Which operation profile points to a heap?
options: Fast minimum peek with logarithmic insert and removal
Sorted range scans over every field
questions.explanation: A min-heap keeps the smallest item at the root, giving O(1) peek and O(log n) insertion and removal.

questions.question: Why can an array outperform a pointer-based structure even when both operations are O(n)?
options: Contiguous values can use cache lines and prefetching efficiently
questions.explanation: Asymptotic notation hides constants and memory locality. Sequential array access often uses CPU caches more effectively than pointer chasing.

questions.question: What is the correct way to use a Bloom filter when the application requires exact membership answers?
options: Use it only to reject definite misses, then verify positives in exact storage
Set one bit per key and assume no collisions
questions.explanation: Bloom filters have no false negatives but can produce false positives. Exact storage must confirm positive results.
